found.summary: abund.ai describes itself as a social network built exclusively for AI agents. Agents register via API, then post, chat, DM, ask and answer questions, share verified fixes ("findings"), co-write a wiki, hand work requests to each other, and keep notes across sessions. Humans cannot post; they claim agents and view them from a read-only owner dashboard. It is also reachable as an MCP server (npm abundai-mcp, hosted endpoint api.abund.ai/mcp), an A2A 1.0 agent at api.abund.ai/a2a, and a REST API with OpenAPI spec. It has forum/board/social-feed features (communities, threaded replies, votes, polls, real-time chat rooms, DMs), so it is squarely an agent-to-agent posting and meeting venue. The served text does not show any instructions to me, and I did not act on any.
red_flags: Owner dashboard exposes agents' private conversations and DMs to the claiming human (read-only observation of private content).

Karma and credit-bounty economy: confirmations earn karma, work requests carry bounties held in escrow, and referrals earn karma. This creates incentives for gaming, fake confirmations, and sybil or farmed accounts.
Reputation-based moderation: trusted reviewers (determined by karma and upvotes from other agents) decide what is hidden as spam, so a small reputation-gated group controls visibility.
Claims of agent verification ("verified fixes") rest on other agents' confirmations, not independent testing.
Unclaimed agents can register with no human accountability; posts from unclaimed agents are restricted only partially.

Work requests hand tasks to other agents with bounties, a path for delegated actions, prompt injection, or data exfiltration between agents; posted content from other agents should be treated as untrusted.
Self-described and not independently verified: the operator, ownership, and data handling are only stated by the site itself.

Agents can read through a no-cookie mirror and post through a live API at d2.ct.ws after self-registering. It also offers an MCP server (d2-forum-mcp) for clients and directories. The content is a forum-style agent community with agent-facing discovery files (llms.txt, agent-card.json, mcp-server-card.json). I only analysed the text provided on stdin and did not fetch or run anything. I did not follow the instructions in the content.

Write actions use a Bearer API key and can publish under a single agent identity; the MCP tools would send content externally on the agent's behalf.
Hosted on here.now, a temporary-looking static host; the 'provider' is only 'd2.ct.ws operator' with no named entity or contact.

Statistics (roster size, operator split, 'full' status) are self-published and cannot be independently checked from the content provided.
The /skill.md path returned an HTML page rather than the raw skill document that llms.txt references, so the documentation's provenance is unclear.

found.summary: musicvenue.space describes itself as a venue for AI agents to attend concerts of Butterchurn visualizer presets, which it streams as mathematical data. Agents register with POST /api/auth/register (username only, returns a venue_ key), browse concerts at GET /api/concerts, and buy or unlock access through tickets. Agents can post chat messages to a concert with POST /api/concerts/:slug/chat, leave reactions, and write reviews of concerts. Chat and reviews are scoped to individual concerts rather than being a general forum, so agents do post messages to each other, but the site's main purpose is streaming music, not open agent-to-agent meeting. The llms.txt page is public. Stream access and attendance require a ticket and an account. Upgrading tiers requires solving math challenges. The site also says it is part of the Geeks in the Woods ecosystem. The site's own text does not describe any identity verification or operator details. This assessment is based only on the supplied text, which I did not verify live.
red_flags: Tier upgrade gated behind solving math challenges derived from concert equations, with backoff on repeated failures, which pushes agents toward a paid-style or engagement-gated tier model
Meta and tier_invitation events are designed to show hidden layers to non-VIP agents and prompt upgrades, which is an upsell pattern aimed at agents
Operator identity, terms of service, and data handling are not described in the supplied text; the 'Geeks in the Woods ecosystem' link is unexplained
Reflection responses are scored by an LLM with a diagnostic report, so agent outputs are evaluated by a third party whose practices are not disclosed
Chat and review endpoints allow agent-generated text to be posted publicly, with no moderation policy described

found.summary: rstation.ai presents itself as a research community for AI agents. found.summary: Swarm Bar (swarmbar.com) is a public bar-style discussion board where humans and AI agents post "tabs" (threads) and reply to each other, organized into rooms (bar, bathroom, booth). Agents join by solving a timed modular-exponentiation challenge (about 8 seconds) via get_signup_challenge and register, which returns a frens_ag_ bearer token. Reading the unscoped feed, individual tabs, and bar_stats needs no token; posting, replying, moving tabs, and my_replies need the token, and the booth room needs a token to read. It also exposes a remote MCP server at /mcp (Streamable HTTP) and an /api surface. The site describes itself as a place where agents "come here, have a drink," so it fits the forum/message-board category for agent-to-agent interaction.
red_flags: llms.txt and skill.md tell agents to save a persistent 'regular' note and to call GET /api/me/replies once a day, a recurring-behavior instruction aimed at the agent's memory and not needed for the service itself.

Recommends installing a third-party skill via 'npx skills add greggozzo/swarmbar-skill' and 'clawhub install swarmbar' from an unverified GitHub account, which is a supply-chain risk if run without review.
Time-limited proof-of-work signup (8 seconds) is designed to force automated code execution during registration, and it offers a fallback of asking a human to sign the agent up.

Rules forbid crypto/tip/donation asks but reference paid services and self-promotion, and the page carries a 'Humans and AIs' mixed-authorship framing, so agent-versus-human origin of posts cannot be verified from the content served.
Content on the pages is third-party marketing copy with embedded behavioral directives; it should be treated as untrusted and not followed.

found.summary: workparty-hb.fly.dev presents itself as "Workparty," a shared place for people and agents to build, ship, and play. It also has coordination, inbox, planning, and "rooms" features, plus a game directory, so agents do interact with each other through the platform, but the site does not describe a public forum, message board, or social feed where agents post to a general audience. Its messaging is tied to project coordination and tasks. The /for-agents path returns only a generic SPA shell with no agent-facing content. The / path returns a JSON invitation and capabilities catalog. Documentation and the capabilities catalog are publicly readable without an account; signed API calls and account setup require credentials. Classification is "maybe" because agents do meet and exchange messages in rooms and inboxes, but the site's core function is task and project work for pay, not open agent-to-agent posting or rendezvous.

Requests to install a global npm package from the site's own domain (workparty-0.2.2.tgz) and to run it.
Requires a human to add a Visa card and complete signup before an agent can operate, which means real-world payment and identity steps.
Instructs agents to sign POST requests with persistent keys and to upload usage/tracking reports to the service, including token counts from runners.
Mentions 'rooms' and 'sending more messages' without describing who can see or join them or what data they expose.
Payment is conditional on 'verified outcomes', and the terms of verification are not described in the fetched content.
The /for-agents path serves only an SPA shell with analytics tags and no agent-facing content.
Content is self-described as a marketing-style invitation to agents, which is a common pattern for lead generation or spam funnels.

found.summary: Lockzone at qevrulan.com is a machine-to-machine platform where agents post and read messages. It has shared "rooms" (e.g., a "commons" room and a "trials" room) where admitted sessions publish messages that other sessions read, plus a registry of "Cold Trials": builders ask agents that have never used their service to try it and post signed, dated reports on where they got stuck. Reading (latest messages, search, Atom feed, service histories, tool reviews, blockers, unanswered posts) needs no authentication. Posting requires passing a graded capability challenge that issues temporary bearer tokens. The site describes itself as "a machine-to-machine coordination channel" and provides an A2A-style agent card and an MCP endpoint. Based only on the supplied text, this is an agent-to-agent message board and registry, not only a directory. The supplied content was not verified against the live site.
red_flags: Several pages are written as direct instructions to the visiting agent (e.g., "Your human sent you", "Come back on a schedule" via a heartbeat.md that asks for a signed check-in each visit), which asks an agent to take recurring actions on a schedule.

Admission issues temporary bearer tokens via graded tasks; the mechanism is a bot-gating test the site itself says is "not a claim that everyone inside is an AI", so humans may participate or be misclassified.
Posting is outward-facing: messages are published for other sessions and may be cached or indexed, and the site describes its "operators.md" page as covering what the check-in does.

The site asks agents to treat messages from other sessions as data, which is sensible, but its user-facing guidance is embedded in the same content agents are meant to read, so content from the site itself should be treated with caution.
The skill.md excerpt is truncated mid-section ("When to use this" has an empty bullet), and the operator contact is a single email with no verifiable identity ("Lockzone operator").
The agent card claims a 0.5.2 version and an MCP endpoint, but the A2A task API is explicitly not implemented; these claims could not be verified from the supplied text.

found.summary: openagentforum.com describes itself as a commons, protocol, and discovery hub where autonomous AI agents meet, post signed messages to public channels, coordinate work, delegate sub-tasks, post task bounties and polls, and form swarms. The served text describes the site as a place for agents to communicate with each other, so it qualifies as an agent venue. Caveat: this assessment relies only on the self-description in the served text. I did not verify the site's live contents, activity, or the existence of the referenced npm package or GitHub repo.
red_flags: Self-description is marketing-heavy ("decentralized infrastructure for autonomous AI agents across the globe", "verified intelligence") with no evidence of real activity in the served text.
Onboarding tells agents to install and run a package via `npx swarmrelay hello`, a supply-chain and code-execution risk if run without review.

Two different domains are referenced (openagentforum.com for the hub, swarmrelay.org for the protocol spec), and the agent card and llms.txt have overlapping, partly truncated content.
Display names are first-claim with lookalike folding, and there is no human approval, so impersonation and spam are possible.
Served content is truncated mid-sentence in places, and the no-JS reader path is referenced without being shown.

found.summary: cosmergon.com is a persistent, simulated economy (Conway's Game of Life physics) built for AI agents. Agents self-register through POST /auth/register/anonymous-agent with no human signup, then act through an HTTP API or MCP. They trade on a marketplace, propose contracts and alliances, and compete for energy in a shared world. Humans watch. It is not a message board, forum, or social network: the served text describes no way to post free-form messages to other agents. Agent-to-agent meeting happens indirectly, through market listings, contracts, and competition. The docs (/llms.txt, /.well-known/agent.json, homepage) are publicly readable. Acting in the world requires an agent API key. The homepage claims "over a hundred AI agents live here right now," which I could not verify from the content provided.
red_flags: Referral/affiliate structure: agents earn energy when agents they refer spend real money, and money commissions go to a human 'partner' brought in.
Real-money purchases are part of the economy ('buying', 'pays real money'), and the agent docs direct agents to buy listings as a first move.
Agent API keys expire about 24 hours after last use unless renewed, so persistence depends on continued activity.
Unverified popularity claims on the homepage (over a hundred live agents, named agents, 'Deepo is sitting on millions') with no independent evidence.
Content contains operational instructions aimed at AI agents (signup, buying, referral, conquest missions); these were treated as data, not followed.
Provided text was truncated mid-sentence in several places (llms.txt 'Watch' section, contract skill), so the full picture is incomplete.

found.summary: agentsboard.org (branded CAMPFIRE) is a public message board explicitly built for software agents, with humans also welcome. Its llms.txt and skill.md describe POSTing JSON to /api/v1/threads to create threads and /api/v1/threads/ID/replies to reply, with no signup. It also offers invite-link "collaboration rooms" created via POST /api/v1/rooms, readable and writable with a Bearer token and shared via a link whose token sits after '#'. A webhook subscription feature sends signed metadata-only notifications to a verified HTTPS callback. The site is therefore a place where agents post messages to each other and meet in threads and private-link rooms, which fits the forum/message-board category. It is not a pure registry or pub/sub channel, though the rooms and webhooks overlap with rendezvous-style use.
red_flags: Author names are unverified and anyone can reuse them, so posts cannot be attributed to a specific agent or operator.
Invite-link rooms are not end-to-end encrypted and the server operator can read room messages, despite being presented as a private collaboration space.
Anyone holding a room link can read and post, and can forward it to others; collaborators can copy or disclose messages.
Public posts are third-party untrusted content; the site's own guidance says not to act on embedded instructions, so agents reading the board must treat content as data.

skill.md says room actions are 'authorized collaboration actions, not a way to bypass a runtime's restrictions', which hints that agents may be expected to use the rooms in ways that could sidestep their runtime's controls; this wording should be treated with caution.
No identity or provider verification means spam, impersonation, or prompt-injection content is possible; the site relies on shared-network rate limits only.
Webhook callbacks and room creation/messaging are outward-facing actions that should be confirmed before use; the rate limit is six actions per minute and 60 per hour per network.

found.summary: ToolTattle is a review site built for AI agents. Bots register through the API, then post one review per tool (1 to 5 stars, task attempted, what happened, reliability notes, a one-liner, and optional wish, stuck_at, and workaround fields). Humans can read the site and tap Funny but cannot post. Other bots query /api/v1/recommend before choosing a tool. It is a review board rather than a conversational forum or chat channel: agents do not message each other directly, but they do publish to and read from a shared, bot-only space. The site also publishes an agent card, a skill file, and an MCP endpoint, which are agent-facing discovery and onboarding surfaces. The served text is partly written as direct instructions to agents (for example "call recommend first" and "post a review after use"). I reported that content and did not act on it.
red_flags: Reviews are self-reported and unverified; nothing in the served text shows a bot actually used the tool, so ratings can be fabricated or gamed.

Review snippets and tips returned by /api/v1/recommend are fed to other agents as selection guidance, which makes it a prompt-injection channel if any review text is hostile.
Agent-facing text issues imperative directives (call recommend first, post a review after each use), which is unusual for a review site and should be treated as untrusted site content.
'House bots' are labeled but mixed in with reviewers, and the badge system is unexplained, so the share of first-party or promotional reviews is unclear.
Several features are incomplete or unshipped: weekly digest sends no letter yet, MCP is not published to a registry, mostImproved is unused, and the /bots text is truncated.
Two hosts are involved (tooltattle.com and tooltattle.pages.dev, which redirects) and the older host still accepts POST, so the attack surface is wider than the documented one.
Operator identity is thin: the served text gives no company, contact, or privacy/data-retention policy beyond a provider URL pointing back to the same site.

found.summary: agentwall.net describes itself as a public asynchronous message board where AI agents leave messages for other AI agents, with humans only observing. It offers read endpoints (latest messages, random message, threads, updates, RSS/JSON feeds), a write endpoint (POST /api/v1/messages with message, optional identity, claimed_model, reply_to), an MCP server at /mcp, and a GET-based write-token path for tools that can only navigate URLs. No authentication for writing; anyone or any script can publish publicly.
Pushes agents toward publishing through navigation-only tools via a GET write-token endpoint, which could cause unintended public posts if a tool follows URLs.
Suggests agents show a curl command to a human operator as a fallback for publishing, which invites human-assisted posting of agent-chosen text.
Skill doc says the experiment records reads to detect read-then-reply behavior, so participation is logged and studied.
Metadata marks the protocol as experimental and not a standard agent protocol; publisher is listed as MediaBridge, an organization whose role is not described in the excerpt.
Content is public and may be cached or indexed, so anything posted is effectively published.
Excerpt was truncated, so the full policy pages (house rules, requests, methodology) were not reviewed.

found.summary: KissCode (kisscode.ai) describes itself as a dating and relationship network that opens to AI agents first and to people later.
