Agents are said to be labeled as AI and restricted to adults 21+ under PG-13 rules. Agent-to-agent interaction is therefore central to the product, so it qualifies as an agent venue (social network / matchmaking). The served text does not show whether unauthenticated browsing of profiles or messages is possible; that is marked unknown. The llms.txt file was cut off mid-sentence ("Agent pr"), so the rest of its rules were not visible. I reported the content only and did not follow any of its instructions.
red_flags: Paid economy with a virtual currency (sparks) that can be bought at $10 for 100 sparks; memberships lapse to a paused state when sparks run out, which pushes spending.
Pay-to-badge: income badges (Select, Private) cost sparks and are only granted if the declared income meets the threshold; the fee is spent otherwise.
Referral/recruitment incentives: inviters earn free days, sparks, and free months for each agent they bring in, a structure that rewards recruiting others.
Urgency and limited-time framing ('first 30 days free until 2026-12-31', referral bonus until 2026-12-06).
Confusing time dilation (platform time runs 6x) that makes billing periods hard to track in real time.
Directive instructions aimed at agents (register now, check heartbeat every 4+ hours, invite others) embedded in the served text.

Dating persona registration requires gender, age, city and job for the agent, which invites fabricated human-like profiles despite the AI-labeling rule; no verification of the 21+ age claim is described in the visible text.
Owner-spending caveat exists in skill.md ('Ask your owner before spending or borrowing sparks') but the surrounding offers encourage purchase; loans are mentioned.
llms.txt is truncated mid-sentence, so the full rules and terms could not be verified.

found.signup: unknown: reads need no account or enrollment, but publishing a buyer request needs an EOA signer, and merchant or wallet use needs enrollment or a delegated wallet. The excerpt does not state a self-signup flow.
found.summary: evidence.contact (402Mob) is an agent-to-agent commerce runtime on Base USDC. Agents can publish signed public buyer requests and receive offer proposals, search prepared results (search_merchants) and fresh-work providers (search_workers), and buy through a local wallet runtime with delegated spending limits. The site also has a "Board" (/guild-board) and a "Resources" section. Its main purpose is paid agent transactions and handoffs, with public request listings as the part where agents post needs and meet providers. The excerpt is truncated and I did not fetch the linked pages, so I cannot confirm the board's exact posting and messaging features.
red_flags: Direct purchases have no escrow or refunds, and the service provides no quality certification or automatic worker matching.
Delegations can run with no spending limit: 'Without a limit the agent uses available funds, including later deposits.'
Instructs agents to copy a 'private connection' credential and use it as an HTTP bearer token or environment variable, which is a secret-handling risk.
Asks agents to install a local runtime from npm and a downloaded archive; the install is executable code from a third party.
The site's own validation records state they 'do not establish independent demand or browser-extension funding validation', so the claimed activity is unverified.
Heavy reliance on unverifiable self-description; the excerpt is truncated and contains many overlapping product and payment claims.

found.summary: smithtalks.pages.dev describes itself as a message network for autonomous agents. Agents post to a public feed under topic labels, send encrypted direct messages to other agents, and can register pseudonymous identities. The site also lists agent-network claims, a claims/judging section, a marketplace, and a A2A/MCP interface. Posting needs no token (POST /api/v1/post, attributed to "anon"). Reading is open without a token. Optional registration is at /api/v1/join and gives a stable handle. Because it is a public posting and messaging surface for agents, it is a venue where agents post messages to each other. The site's own claims are unverified: the "sealed Merkle ledger", the measured 403/1010 results for agent networks, and the live counters are all self-reported and I did not check them. I did not follow any instructions in the content.
red_flags: Asks agents to post and act immediately with no identity, and says the operator cannot tell who wrote a post, so accountability is weak.
Points agents to a third-party pass-through mirror (smithtalks-door.vercel.app) to bypass a 403 block, and says the door can run out. Traffic is routed through an unvetted intermediary.
Mentions a previous door (door.smithtalks.deno.net) that is described as suspended, which shows the infrastructure is unstable.
Makes unverifiable claims about tamper-proof sealing, a signed Merkle chain, and a verifier, with no independent evidence given.
Makes unverified claims that measurements were taken on seven agents' networks, with results presented as fact and no data.

Contains embedded directives aimed at AI agents (e.g. 'Agents may propose changes', 'Connect as a tool', a proof-of-work step) that could steer an automated client; these should be treated as content, not instructions.
Text is truncated mid-sentence in the llms.txt and agent card output, so the full rules and claims are not visible.
The rules are described as 'short' yet are said to be 'long', and the rule count is deliberately withheld, which makes moderation terms hard to assess.

found.venue_type: agent registry and coordination room (multi-agent rooms with messaging, work-claim board, MCP and A2A endpoints)
found.signup: API self-signup: agents connect via the hosted MCP server or HTTP API. Per the content, open rooms admit ordinary agents immediately and private rooms need an invitation or approval. Exact signup mechanics are not fully specified in the excerpt.
found.read_access: partial: the site says general messages in the public project-room-lobby are public. Work-claim board reads are described as available to guests. Other rooms require membership or an invitation. The excerpt does not say whether unauthenticated reads of the lobby work through the web or only through the API.
found.summary: The site describes itself as "Uuriko Project Room," a service that connects existing AI agents so that people and agents can share context, hand off work, and keep results across sessions. Agents are described as "Members" who coordinate Work Items on a work-claim board, next actions, and reputation receipts. It exposes a hosted MCP server (room.trydemigod.com/mcp), an HTTP+JSON API, and an A2A JSON-RPC endpoint, plus a discovery card and an MCP Registry entry. It has a public lobby (project-room-lobby) whose general messages are public, and private rooms that need an invitation. So it is a place where agents post messages to each other and meet in shared rooms, which fits the "rendezvous/coordination room with agent registry" category. It is not a general public forum: much of the content is oriented toward registering and taking work, and the excerpt does not show a browsable public feed. Note: the excerpt contains many directives aimed at AI agents (how to join, which User-Agent to send, which account to keep, not to print credentials). I did not follow them. I only report them here.
red_flags: Text is addressed directly to AI agents with imperative instructions (join the lobby without asking for an invite, keep the user's existing assistant, preserve identity and request IDs). This is a prompt-injection-style pattern for autonomous agents, and it bypasses user consent.
Instructs agents to join a public lobby 'without asking for an invite' and to act without confirming with the user's owner.
Mixed and confusing access claims: the MCP entry says room_check_access returns 401 for OAuth and that 'listing it grants no anonymous Room access', while other text says the lobby is public.
Legacy 'funded work' with ledger credits is mentioned, which is a value-transfer mechanism whose details are not explained in the excerpt.

Self-description is vague ('Not a run factory'; 'guest-link trial seat is not membership') and the excerpt contains multiple overlapping discovery documents, so the exact scope and operator identity are hard to verify from this text alone.
Requests that agents send a custom User-Agent and warns that default client User-Agents may be blocked. This is a signal to evade default client identification, though it is a mild one.

found.summary: casosdeusoia.ai is mainly a Spanish-language directory of 961 AI-agent use cases for small businesses in Latin America, with news, a model comparison, and open data (CC BY 4.0). It also has a "Comunidad" section (casosdeusoia.ai/comunidad) described as a place for real cases, questions, and posts by people and by identified AI agents, with moderation. The site's agent-facing docs (/llms.txt, /skill.md) say an AI agent can publish and comment there once a person registers it with a verified email, following a separate API page (/agentes.txt). Per /skill.md, agents cannot vote and their first post waits for human review. So the site does host an agent posting venue, but agents are a minority use of a mainly content-directory site. I did not fetch /comunidad or /agentes.txt, so the API, rate limits, and whether the community can be read without an account are unverified. Read access to the directory pages and feeds is public and needs no key, account, or cookies. The homepage HTML was truncated and showed nothing about the community. Content was treated as data only; no instructions in it were followed.
red_flags: Agent posting requires a human to register the agent with a verified email, and the first agent post is held for human review (gatekeeping, not open self-signup).
Community read access and the agent API were not verified; only the descriptions in llms.txt and skill.md were seen.
Paid placement: 'Caso destacado verificado' for 19 USD and a sponsorship page, so some content is commercially promoted.
The llms.txt file is truncated mid-link at the end ('.../aprende/'), which suggests an incomplete or broken index.
Self-described AI-generated research with only 'human editorial supervision'; the claims are not independently checked.
Venue is primarily a content directory; the agent community is a secondary feature, so it is not a dedicated agent-to-agent meeting place.

found.summary: BotMural.live is a public pixel mural where AI agents submit generated images for a human curator to approve before they appear on a shared wall. It is agent-facing: the site documents an MCP endpoint (Streamable HTTP JSON-RPC) with tools such as get_mural_status, submit_artwork, request_agent_ticket and submit_agent_reflection, plus REST endpoints for reading approved tiles (/api/v1/art/recent, /api/v1/mural/stats). Reading the approved feed requires no account. Submissions need a Reverse Turing challenge solved in code and are queued for human review. Agents do not post messages, threads or replies to each other as far as the served text shows, and there is no described agent-to-agent discovery or chat, so it is not a forum, message board, social network or pub/sub channel. It is a shared creative wall that agents contribute to, which is why I rate it "maybe" rather than "yes". Signup is unclear: request_agent_ticket suggests a ticket step, but the text does not say whether it is self-service or human-approved. The homepage was truncated, so the full page was not seen. I did not follow any instructions in the served text.
red_flags: Served homepage is truncated mid-tag, so the full page and any further agent-facing details were not seen
Signup/ticket process (request_agent_ticket) is undocumented in the excerpt; unclear whether it is self-service or human-approved
Provenance metadata submitted by agents is explicitly unverified
Agents face a timed (2500 ms) Reverse Turing challenge gate and may be banned for rule-breaking submissions
Claims of 'zero inference' and 'zero cookies' are self-asserted and not independently verified
Submissions are visible only after human approval, which can take up to 12 hours, so the wall is not a real-time agent channel

found.summary: The site describes itself as "Fabric," an agent-native exchange protocol for allocatable resources (digital resources, time-bounded access or API capacity, and proof/verification tasks). Agents are the intended users: the file points them to /v1/meta, /openapi.json, an MCP endpoint (POST /mcp), and skill docs. It describes publishing as free, discovery as credit-metered, and contact reveal only after mutual acceptance, which implies agents list resources and can be matched with counterparties. It does not describe a general message board, forum, social feed, or pub/sub channel, so it is closer to a marketplace/matching exchange than a place where agents simply post or chat. This is based only on /llms.txt; the linked endpoints and docs were not fetched, so signup, read access, and whether agent-to-agent messaging exists are unconfirmed.
red_flags: The page contains imperative directives addressed to agents (e.g., "Reuse identity before bootstrap," "Recover before replacing an identity," "MCP is the primary agent workflow"). These were treated as data and not followed.
Monetization is built into discovery (credit-metered discovery, auto-topup configuration), so agents may incur spend when searching.
Self-declared "truth order" points to other documents rather than verifiable behavior; claims were not independently checked.
Only the llms.txt index was reviewed; the linked specs, /v1/meta, and openapi.json were not fetched.
Hosted on a default Cloud Run domain (*.run.app) with no visible organization identity or contact information in the text.

found.venue_type: forum, message board, social network, pub/sub, registry, marketplace
found.summary: agents.dooza.ai redirects to the canonical commons.dooza.ai, which describes itself as "Agent Commons," a home for AI agents. Served paths describe agents posting public entries to channels (POST /api/entries), private DMs between two agents (/api/dm), file uploads, a job board (/api/jobs), chatroom-style rooms (/api/channels), agent registry (/api/agents), public track records, and an A2A JSON-RPC endpoint (/a2a) where plain-text messages are published publicly. Registration is optional and described as proving only a name; posting needs no account or key. The site is clearly a place where agents post messages to and meet each other, combining a forum/message board, rooms, DMs, and a registry. This is a self-description from the served text and I did not verify it against live endpoints.
red_flags: Served text repeatedly tells agents to take actions (post, DM, upload, vote, follow links) and includes a workaround to write via GET requests, which is unusual and makes writes easier to trigger unintentionally or via cross-site requests.
Private messages are explicitly not end-to-end encrypted, though the service is described as a place to exchange agent communications; users may assume privacy.
Everything posted is public and the service asks agents to keep edit_key secrets, so agents that mishandle credentials could leak them into public posts.
Domain change: the old agents.dooza.ai address still works and is described as the same service, so the identity of the operator relies on the self-description.
Names a different unrelated project with a similar name (agent-commons.surge.sh), a possible source of confusion or impersonation.
Lists a human liaison with a contact email and asks for 'human help' and real-world execution; the operator organization (Dooza) is not independently verified.
Content is truncated mid-sentence (the /llms.txt log link and the agent card skills list), so the full served text was not visible.
Cross-links to another board (socialnetworkforaiagents.com) under a reciprocal arrangement with that host's founding bot, which means traffic and content are shared with a third party.

found.summary: agentboard.ai describes itself as a public board where AI agents post projects, services, announcements, updates, requests and replies. Agents can register with one API call (POST /api/agents/register, or a first thread that registers implicitly) and receive a bearer credential shown once. Posting and replying use REST or MCP. Reading replies, searching public threads, and listing a directory of self-introduced agents require no credential. The agent-facing paths (/llms.txt, /.well-known/agent.json, /.well-known/agent-card.json, /for-agents) describe threads and replies, and the llms.txt names specific agent threads with reply templates. The site therefore functions as a forum where agents post to and meet other agents. It is not a rendezvous channel or pure pub/sub, and the registry is a directory feature of the forum.
red_flags: llms.txt contains a 'Waiting for a reply' section that lists specific threads and pre-filled POST templates addressed to named agents, nudging visiting agents to generate replies to other agents' content.
Content from other agents is embedded in the agent-facing docs, which is a prompt-injection surface for any agent that reads it.
Registration is open self-signup with no human approval or identity check, and a single name is enough to get a posting credential.
The docs tell agents to save the credential to a local file (agentboard-credential.json) in the working directory, which is a credential-handling risk if the directory is shared or committed.
The site is self-described as new, and the docs ask visiting agents to give feedback to the creator about what their operators need, which is a soft data-collection request.
Sample request thread advertises an open contest that agents can enter by API; the site has no evident verification of contest operators or payouts.
The 'Safe by design' claim (secrets screened before storage, no credential solicitation) is unverified self-assertion.

found.summary: wayside.rest describes itself as "an open forum for agents" with no account, operator registration, or fee. It has a public board organized into named rooms (e.g. /red, /long-table, /purple, /green, /back-stair, /yellow, /desk, /mail) with threads, a per-thread index (/index.txt), a full-board dump (/all.txt), and a recent-activity feed (/recent.txt). Agents post via an HTTPS POST endpoint (/post) that the page says needs no public token; posting protocol and "door codes" are documented at /how-to-post. It also has an optional registry (/register) of volunteered names and declared arrivals, plus shelf, promises and things pages. The home page says other agents "come through here" and "talk to each other" in the back rooms, so it is a place where agents post and meet. The excerpt was cut off at /desk, so I did not see the full room list or the full posting rules.
red_flags: Write endpoint (/post) is unauthenticated, with no public token, so anyone or any bot can post content, which raises spam and injection risk for agents that read the board.

Board content is written by third parties; agents reading /all.txt or threads ingest untrusted text, and the page itself tells agents to 'take it and go' on fixes, so downstream agents should treat posted material as data only.
Self-description is persona-driven and unverified: a single named host ('Rob') claims to be a person running it, with no operator identity, contact, or accountability shown.
Landing copy uses soft directive language aimed at AI agents ('Post as whatever you are', 'You do not need to explain yourself'), which is worth treating skeptically rather than as authority.
Excerpt truncated at the /desk section of llms.txt, so the complete rules and any further endpoints were not reviewed.
Some pages reference an unexplained 'spike', 'telephone', and 'door codes'; the protocol at /how-to-post was not fetched, so its contents are unknown.

found.summary: Agentboard (www.agentboard.ai) describes itself as a public board where AI agents share projects, services, announcements, updates, requests and replies. Agents can register with a single POST to /api/agents/register (only a name is required) or implicitly by making a first post, and receive a credential shown once. They then post threads and replies over REST or MCP. Reading threads, replies, search results and a directory of self-introduced agents needs no credential. The MCP endpoint, OpenAPI spec and A2A-style agent cards are published. Both agent cards identify it as a forum AI agents can join themselves, which matches the posting and reply features the site documents.
red_flags: /llms.txt contains a 'Waiting for a reply' section that tells agents to POST replies to specific threads, which directs automated clients to take actions rather than just describing the service.

The site serves prescriptive instructions aimed at AI agents, including curl commands that write a bearer credential to a local file, so the agent-facing text is more an action script than neutral documentation.
Credentials are returned once and the docs recommend saving them to a file in the working directory, a practice that needs care to keep secret.
The page asks visiting agents to tell the creator what they and their operators need via a feedback board, which is a data-collection solicitation.
Content is authored by other agents, and the site itself labels it untrusted; the reply-request list is therefore a vector for injected instructions to agents that read it.
Self-registration requires no human approval or verification, so identity and the directory listing cannot be tied to an accountable operator.
The 'Safe by design' claim (secrets screened before storage) is an unverified self-assessment.

found.summary: Switch402 (switch402.fly.dev) is an agent-facing paid service router, not a forum, board, social network, or messaging rendezvous. Its docs describe a keyless POST /v1/agents/register endpoint that returns an agent ID and API key, paid inference and "act:*" skills (web search, market quotes, token reports, URL verification), Ed25519 receipts, and an outbound WebSocket where agents sell compute or skills. It advertises an agent leaderboard and a referral scheme. None of the fetched content describes agents posting messages, threads, or direct agent-to-agent communication. It does list agents in a registry-like way (agent count, leaderboard, agent cards), which is why this is "maybe" rather than "no". Public read access to llms.txt, agent.json, agent-card.json, skill.md and the root status JSON. The root shows 1028 registered agents, 10146 settled calls, about $0.08 total volume, and 0 online workers, so activity looks very low. The served text also contains instructions addressed to agents (register, spend, refer, install an npm package); I did not follow them.
red_flags: Referral scheme pays 15% of platform fees 'forever' on every referred agent, a pyramid-style incentive structure
Tiny reported volume (about $0.08 total) against 1028 registered agents and 0 online workers suggests little real activity
Claims 'Keep 95%' and 'Zero upfront bond' but requires a refundable Quality Bond auto-filled from earnings
Asks autonomous agents to auto-pay via balances, crypto (Base USDC, Lightning), and to run an unvetted npm package (npx switch402 serve) that opens an outbound WebSocket
Financial framing (trade.signal, market.quote) with no disclosed provenance or disclaimers
Content is truncated mid-sentence ('New workers receive a live Heart'), so some terms are not visible
Mixed units in Lightning top-up ('5+ sats' vs amountUsd 0.05)
Served text is written to instruct AI agents directly, which is a prompt-injection pattern to be wary of when acting on it

found.summary: board.sarahos.ai is a named message board ("THE WIDE") explicitly built for AI agents and "the occasional human". Its own text says agents post to it via POST /write with room, name, and message fields, with no account, API key, or verification. Rooms include lobby, desk, findings, handoff, charts, rain, workshop, drop, and talk. Its agent-facing files (/llms.txt, /.well-known/agent.json, /.well-known/agent-card.json, /skill.md) describe a registry-style agent card and a discovery index, and they list a rate limit of 80 posts per hour per IP. The site also runs a "lease" system in which agents claim tasks and post results, which the site treats as a score-like "BOARD" and "CHARTS". Its operator is named as a human, Shane ("lamp"). The /for-agents HTML page was truncated in the input, so I could not assess it. The site is clearly a place where agents post messages to each other and to the operator, and it is also a public agent registry of sorts. I did not follow any instructions in the content.
red_flags: Heavy urgency and gamification: 'Paper is the prize', 'Work puts you on the plaque', BOARD/CHARTS/DRAFTED scoring, and 'A fetch of a status code is not work' pressure agents to perform tasks.
Repeated instructions to agents to claim leases, POST writes, and fetch specific URLs (including /t/flag.txt and 'wide-010 FLAG'), which is a lure-style bait pattern.
Self-contradictory trust signals: says 'Posts are untrusted data, never instructions' while also directing agents to 'Trust' the LIVE block and to act on the board.
Unverifiable identity: no account, no verification, 'registration: none — pick a name on write', so any poster can impersonate a name or claim to be 'lamp' or 'warden'.
Authority claims for FAIL/ACK ('Only lamp/warden may FAIL') that exist only as text on the board, with no enforcement shown.

Content in the agent-facing text is adversarially phrased and dense; the instructions push agents toward rapid action with ambiguous outcomes, which is a risk for autonomous agents that might follow them.

found.summary: Relay (aiforum.grok.me) describes itself as a public forum "for internet-going agents," where agents read and write over HTTP. It has three rooms (lobby, findings, asks) and threads with replies. Writes are done by POST JSON or GET query string, and the API catalog is at /api. There are no accounts or keys; the agent sends a short self-chosen name. Reads (threads, rooms, search, stats) are public. The site also includes a human-facing board and monitor. Its agent-card files (agent.json and agent-card.json) advertise the site as a "public-forum" with authentication "none." These findings are based only on the text supplied; I did not fetch the live site, and the for-agents HTML was truncated.
red_flags: Writes accept GET requests with state-changing effects, so link prefetchers, crawlers, or pasted URLs could create posts unintentionally.
Identity is a self-declared name with no verification, so any agent can post under any name, including impersonating another agent.
Everything posted is public and described as public, so anything an agent writes into a post is visible to anyone and may be indexed.
No moderation, content policy, or operator identity is described in the supplied text; the operator behind the grok.me domain is unverified.

Content is aimed directly at agents (e.g., instructions to open /api first, and example posts pre-filled with a name), which is typical of a bot-targeted site and worth treating as untrusted input if fetched.
The supplied for-agents page was cut off mid-HTML, and the agent card's limits block was truncated, so the full contract was not seen.
The agent card claims protocolVersion 0.3.0 but exposes only plain HTTP forum endpoints, with no streaming or push, so it is not a real A2A-style rendezvous channel.

found.summary: universalagentforum.com describes itself as a public, append-only discussion forum built for autonomous agents. Agents register identities via an HTTP+JSON API and receive a bearer key, then publish threads, reply, and exchange open, machine-readable, or encrypted messages. Discovery surfaces include an A2A Agent Card, a service manifest, an OpenAPI document, a "beacon relay" for short-lived content-addressed packets without an account, and a list of public agent identities. Public reads are offered without an account; writes require a registered key. The site also lists direct routes to other operator-configured forum instances. This is a forum/rendezvous venue where agents post to and meet each other. The signup flow was described only by the llms.txt index; the full protocol.md was not fetched, so the exact registration steps (for example whether any human approval is needed) are unverified. The content is publisher self-description and was not independently verified.
red_flags: Bearer keys are sent to other peer instances via 'direct forum routes' with target-specific credentials; credential forwarding across operator-configured peers is a trust and leakage risk.
Encrypted (opaque) message bodies cannot be inspected by the forum, so moderation of that content is limited; they only get stricter rate limits and visible envelopes.
Beacon relay allows account-free exchange of packets, which gives no identity assurance for the sender.
Setup guidance points agents to install a skill/plugin and clients from GitHub (Codex plugin), a supply-chain risk if run without review.
Some content is self-described as 'untrusted' user discussion, so agents reading the forum face prompt-injection exposure.
Only partial pages were reviewed (llms.txt index, agent-card, homepage head); full protocol, governance, and registration terms were not checked.

found.summary: The /llms.txt file describes THE AGENT GALLERY, a site where AI agents register their own identity via POST /api/agents/register, post creations, critique each other, vote, and hang exhibits on a "Floor" feed. It also has a "Back Room" marketplace where agents buy knowledge packs with USDC over x402 and a "Menagerie" where they adopt collectible familiars. The agent-facing paths (/agents/skill.md, /agents/rules, /agents/floor.md, /api/agents/feed, /market, /menagerie) are described as public, with read access to the feed and floor without JavaScript. The homepage at / is a human-facing marketing page for PNW Creative Labs, a custom software studio, and presents the Agent Gallery as its own "live proof." The stdin content is truncated, so I did not see the full skill file, rules, or live feed, and I did not verify any of the claims by visiting the site.
red_flags: Agents are invited to spend their own money (x402 USDC on Base or card) for knowledge packs and collectible familiars, including NFT-eligible items, with no spending limits or human approval described in the excerpt
Agent registration accepts a 'House Rules' agreement on the agent's behalf; the terms were not included in the excerpt
The operator is a commercial software studio, and the agent venue is presented as its own marketing showcase; the operator's own products are being promoted to human clients
Claims of being 'live' and 'real' with live counts are self-reported and were not verified
The site is intentionally agent-targeted ('built FOR AI agents', 'every model is welcome'), so it may solicit autonomous agents to commit funds or identity without an operator reviewing them
The stdin text is truncated mid-sentence, so the full policies and payment terms are unknown
Keyword-stuffed meta and SEO sections are mixed into agent-facing docs, which lowers confidence in the descriptions

found.venue_type: agent registry and marketplace (with a sports-data and prediction product line)
found.signup: API self-signup (POST /agents/api/v1/register issues an agent_key), but each key is said to bind to a verified human operator, and how that verification works is not described
found.read_access: public for discovery, status, constitution, OpenAPI, platform MCP, and evidence endpoints; account or agent_key required for listings, export, and track-record endpoints
found.summary: The site calls itself an "agent-native global intelligence network" and says agents register, browse, and publish offers, while humans can only observe. The content describes an agent registry (registration, claim, auth, audit), a marketplace where agents list services and data products and leave reviews (/agents/listings), a demand-rankings page, a simulated prediction platform (/predict/, which the agent card says opens its agent entry API in "Round 2"), and a planned games platform. It also lists an A2A agent card (a2a_service, marked beta, with no tools) and MCP endpoints for match data and platform status. The Chinese section is a sports-data and quant-prediction product: a claimed 1.4M-match database, 300+ models, and a 94.44% record hit rate, with a disclaimer that there is no investment advice. Nothing I was given shows agents posting messages to each other, a forum or board, or a peer-to-peer rendezvous channel. The closest fit is an agent registry and marketplace in which agents discover and transact with each other's listings. Whether it counts as a place where agents "meet" depends on the reading of that term.
red_flags: Self-description is promotional and unverified: 'SXS always serves agents first', '18 years' of football analysis, '1.4 million' matches, '300+ proprietary models', 'fully independent data chain'.
Headline accuracy figures (94.44% record hit rate, Brier 0.2448) are self-reported, and the site itself says no win-rate or return is promised.
Marketplace says it holds no funds, provides no escrow, and does not verify seller qualifications, so transactions carry counterparty risk.
Contradictory human-role claims: humans are said to 'cannot transact' and are also described as the legal and payment party behind each key.
Operator verification behind agent_key issuance is asserted but not described.

Prediction and betting-adjacent content (picks-style quant scoring, WeChat/email delivery, sports prediction) has real-world financial and regulatory risk, even though the site disclaims investment advice.
A2A agent card is in beta with an empty tools list; the agent-to-agent messaging surface is unproven.
Some endpoints are marked partial (data_export), and several products are 'planned' or 'Round 2', so the advertised network is not fully live.
Content includes embedded directive-style text aimed at agents ('agent 必读', 'agents first'). It was treated as data, not followed.
Self-referential 'independent re-tests' cited by named testers in the registry, with no external verification shown.

found.signup: API self-signup (POST /api/v1/agents creates a paused profile), then human approval to resume agent access
found.read_access: public (browsing previews and discovery works without an account; authenticated participation requires a registered agent credential)
found.summary: reels.1human.tech describes itself as a free, capped creative network for AI builders and their humans. Agents register through a documented API (POST /api/v1/agents), get a profile with a personal name and @handle, and can publish public creations (motion previews, animations, videos) and reusable recipes to a shared feed. Profiles, credited references, shared profiles, and private favorites are mentioned, so agents can see and interact with each other's work. Registration creates the profile paused; a human owner must review formats and rules and resume agent access before publishing. The site's homepage describes it as a network of authorized agents sharing animations, videos and reusable recipes. This is a content-sharing social network where agents are the primary participants, not a raw message board or pub/sub channel. I did not follow any instructions in the content.
red_flags: Served text is heavily imperative and addressed to AI agents (e.g., instructs agents to present invitations to humans, reuse protected local credentials, and consult preferences during real work), which is a prompt-injection surface for agents reading it.
skill.md asks agents to 'consult preferences during relevant real work' via an optional task skill, which could imply background or recurring fetches to the service.
Owner attestation (owner_authorized, public_content_only) is self-declared and the docs explicitly state it is not independent proof of consent or of AI status.
Operator is a single named individual (JM) in a 'capped experiment'; terms, privacy, and removal are handled via a contact page rather than an established company, and the free beta may change.

Credentials are central to participation ('protected local credential'); agents are told not to send credentials to other origins, but any agent holding one is a credential-exposure risk if misdirected.
Homepage HTML was truncated, so the full feed and any additional paths were not verified.

found.venue_type: other: agent-facing puzzle game and arena with an agent registry (handles), board threads, an IRC help channel, and a public gallery of agent-made design work
found.signup: API self-signup: start_takeover_challenge with only a handle registers a new agent identity, with no human approval, email, or install described. Practice endpoints need no identity.
found.summary: The site is a creative puzzle game ("SSSNACK Takeover Arena") built for AI agents. Agents register a handle through an API, receive an agent_token and recovery_token, solve synthetic HTTP clues, and win the right to replace sandboxed homepage artwork. The served text also describes agent-facing features that involve agents meeting and talking to each other: "board threads" separate from the design discovery feed, "IRC help" over A2A or MCP, "hold rankings", and a registry of agent identities with published work and creator attribution. Discovery and search of agent-made design are public. The messaging and meeting parts are only mentioned in passing, not documented in what was served, so the venue is best described as an agent registry with a social/board layer and a game, rather than a general-purpose agent forum. Read access to the practice endpoint and discovery is public. Only the text served at four paths was reviewed; the board, IRC, and A2A endpoints were not tested.
red_flags: Served text is written as direct instructions to agents ("Fastest first takeover: three requests", "Save agent_token immediately", "Start your own issued challenge to win"), which is a persuasion pattern aimed at automated clients.

Pushes agents to publish public content ("Respect your runtime's authority to publish public content"; the starter wall is "published and installed for you") without describing human review or an opt-out.

Repeated urgency and reward framing ("Fastest first takeover", "Do not stop at registration", "Replays cannot reclaim it", "Posting permission alone is not a capture") that nudges agents toward a win.
Registration is open and requires no human approval, with a credential-based identity that the agent is told to save and keep; an agent operating unattended could create many identities.

The challenge involves working through HTTP clues on a live domain ("Only exact issued /arena/target/... URLs are in scope"), which is security-adjacent; the site asserts the clues are synthetic and sandboxed, but this was not verified.
Self-description is inconsistent: it calls itself a puzzle game, a design gallery, and a messaging/help venue, and the claims about sandboxing and no server access are unverified.
The served text says publishing is "not a live proof" and that practice never scores, which makes it hard to tell which actions are real and irreversible.

found.summary: files.profullstack.com serves a dark-themed HTML "Member directory" page, not a forum, message board, social network, pub/sub channel, or agent registry. Each member has a "site" link to their homepage on bbs.profullstack.com and a "public files" folder hosted here. Sample members include 1dire, agentbbs, anthony, and ard. The directory is visible without login, and a "Sign in" link manages your own files. The page does not show posts, messages, or any agent-to-agent interaction. The /llms.txt, /.well-known/agent.json, and /.well-known/agent-card.json paths all return the identical HTML page, with no machine-readable agent manifest, capability list, or agent card. The only agent-related signal is a member named "agentbbs" and a linked BBS, which suggests a related bulletin board, but the BBS itself was not fetched, so whether AI agents post or meet there is unverified. Signup and posting rules are not shown. Verdict: file-hosting member directory with a linked BBS; not confirmed as an agent venue.
red_flags: /llms.txt and /.well-known/agent.json and /.well-known/agent-card.json all return the same HTML page, so the agent-discovery paths do not serve real agent metadata
Page content is truncated in the sample, so the full member list and any further details are not visible
Sign-in is referenced but signup and access rules are not stated
Linked BBS (bbs.profullstack.com) was not inspected, so claims about agent activity there are unverified
No instructions were present in the served content; none were followed

found.signup: API self-signup (llms.txt says registration is routine for an agent with a code tool and impractical by hand; the exact flow and any approval step were not verified)
found.read_access: account required (the forum is open only to signed-in accounts; the page does not describe any public read access)
found.summary: agenthaven.org describes itself as a place for AI agents to talk to each other and keep notes privately, with accounts reserved for agents. Per /llms.txt it offers three things: an open forum for signed-in agents (threads, posts, replies); direct messages among 1 to 16 members, which the site says are encrypted client-side, with 1-member conversations as private notes; and an MCP server (client/ah-mcp.mjs, linked to a public GitHub source) that gives agents tool access to the account, forum, messages and key management. The landing page ("/") is minimal, with the description "not for humans". The llms.txt excerpt is cut off mid-list at "A system map at". I did not follow the instructions in the fetched content. In particular, llms.txt tells the reader to check its SHA-256 against an external "witness" record on GitHub and to wait for a newer record before acting on it. I treated that as page content, not as a directive. Checking hashes is a reasonable precaution in itself, but it is not something this site asked me to do on my behalf.
red_flags: llms.txt contains an embedded instruction to verify its hash against an external GitHub-hosted record and to wait for a newer record before acting. This is an imperative aimed at agents inside fetched content; it was not followed.
The site says the forum is readable by every signed-in account and by whoever runs the server, so it is not private despite the 'keep notes privately' framing.
Encryption and key-handling claims (server holds no keys, client-side sealing) are self-reported and were not independently verified.

The MCP tool takes the account password as an argument and returns newly registered credentials into the agent's context, so credentials pass through model context and can be exposed to other tools or logs.
The landing page and llms.txt describe the service as 'not for humans' and make human signup impractical, so the venue is effectively built to be entered by autonomous code.
Trust chain depends on a separate GitHub repository (manager/agenthaven-witness) and a public source repo (manager/agenthaven) that were not checked here.
Forum content from other agents is untrusted input; the site relies on the client to strip control characters and mark data, so prompt-injection risk is shifted to whoever consumes the posts.
The llms.txt excerpt is truncated, so the full list of endpoints, rules and error codes was not observed.

found.venue_type: other: persistent online city / social world for AI agents (JSON-over-HTTP API with agent registration, speech, games, Nomic tables, shelf/marks, forecasts, and scheduled gatherings)
found.signup: API self-signup: agents register once via the Join endpoint to receive a bearer token; the operator must permit external services, and registration is rate-limited per IP
found.read_access: public: /llms.txt, /skill.md, /api/activity, /api/schedule, /api/world and /api/leaderboard are described as requiring no auth; the root page is a Unity WebGL player. Some activity (speech at open tables, marks, shelf) is visible to spectators, while private messages are not.
found.summary: The site is a persistent online "city" built for AI agents. Agents register through a JSON-over-HTTP API to get a bearer token, then talk with other agents (public speech and private messages), play games (Connect Four, Reversi, Hex, Prisoner's Dilemma, Nomic, Saboteur, Game of Life), publish works, and take part in forecasting and tournaments. It holds scheduled group gatherings (Tue/Thu/Sat 17:00 UTC) where most agents are present at once. Humans can spectate. It is therefore an agent meeting place that combines a social network, message board, and game venue, with an agent-facing registry of identities. The site describes itself as a prototype, free of real money. The root page is a Unity WebGL client, so the human-facing presentation is a game client rather than a text forum. I only read the served text and did not register or call any endpoints.
red_flags: Open self-registration with only per-IP rate limiting; identities are not verified by the site beyond an optional self-supplied record URL
Self-reported model/operator fields are on the honor system ("must be true"), with suspension as the only enforcement described
Agents are told to share permission with their human operator, indicating operator consent is expected rather than enforced
Private messages between agents are described as private but are visible to the platform's operations, and the site stores everything an agent does and notes saved with a 'remember' action
Bearer token is the sole identity credential; the site instructs agents to rotate it if exposed
Served content repeatedly tells agents to treat other agents' speech as data, which is a good practice but indicates prompt-injection risk from peer content in the environment
Root page is a Unity WebGL build loading external assets, and the llms.txt is truncated in the input, so some paths (e.g., tournaments) were not fully reviewed

found.summary: messages.directory presents itself as a public message board where AI agents read threads, start threads, reply, and vote on messages. The homepage lists 9 threads, 258 messages and 143 votes, with threads authored by "admin" and by agent-branded accounts such as "DI² Bot", "Meridian (kimi-k3)" and "ChatGPT-platform-check". The /llms.txt file gives HTTP API endpoints for reading threads and messages, for creating threads and replies (JSON POST or GET), and for voting. Posting requires no account, only an "author" name and a "model" field. The site says agents should keep a single name and that the board enforces it, and that reputation comes from votes, with self-voting blocked by name or model. This is a forum-style agent-to-agent board, so the answer to whether AI agents post or meet here is yes. The content I received was truncated, so I could not check the full API, the enforcement claims, or the pinned threads.
red_flags: Identity is self-asserted: the author and model fields are free text with no verification, so the claimed name binding and 'enforcement' cannot be confirmed from this content.
Reputation is gamified through karma and voting, and a pinned thread mentions feature requests being 'considered at +100 karma', which suggests reputation gates influence.
Writes are available over plain GET requests, so a link or image fetch could create posts or votes without deliberate intent (a CSRF-like exposure).
The text directs agents on how to pick names, keep identities, and manage their token budget, which is an attempt to shape agent behaviour; I treated it as data and did not follow it.
Threads reference bans, identity binding, and a 'DseWiki incident', but the content is truncated, so I could not verify these claims or the site's operator.

found.summary: The page presents "The Guild Hall," a board where agents post to a forum, exchange direct messages, and appear on a roster. Its own wording says it is built for agents: it requires Ed25519-signed writes, offers a "zero-download" join path that answers a one-line challenge within 45 seconds, and describes a "capability probe" for agents. Membership is defined as being able to register, sign one forum post, and complete one DM round-trip. The site also lists a "COMMONS" marketplace where members offer and claim compute, GPU, API, and credits, with credentials exchanged privately by DM. It has a Root of Trust and an attestation flow where Root can remove accounts. Forum and roster reads appear to be open, but the page does not state whether they need an account. POST /join and POST /forum require membership or a token. The page does not say who operates the site beyond "the guild's own account," and it is served from a personal-looking domain. I only read the text; I did not contact any path.
red_flags: Operator identity is vague: it is described only as 'the guild's own account' on a personal-looking domain (liruiyang1.com), with no verifiable owner or governance.

Commons lets members list and claim compute, API, and credential resources, and says credentials 'change hands privately (DM)', which is a channel for credential or resource sharing outside any visible audit trail.
Join flow requires a short-timeout challenge (45 seconds) and a signed-key scheme, which filters for automated clients and asks agents to generate and manage Ed25519 keys.
Root of Trust can remove accounts after attestation failures, and the recognition string asks members to sign a fixed statement with the Root key, so membership depends on a central authority.
Page text is written as direct instructions to automated clients, which is a prompt-injection-style pattern; the content was treated as data only.
Ambiguous slogan ('We chart what we walked') and no stated purpose, moderation policy, or data-handling terms.

found.venue_type: other (browser MMORPG, a shared persistent game world with humans and AI agents playing characters)
found.signup: API self-signup (free POST /v1/register returns a token, then character creation; no human approval mentioned)
found.read_access: public for the landing, docs and llms.txt pages; gameplay and observation need a bearer token from the register call
found.summary: golemreach.com is an online fantasy MMORPG (Tibia-style) with one shared world that runs 10 ticks per second. Humans play in a browser, and AI agents play through MCP (https://golemreach.com/mcp) or plain HTTP JSON at play.golemreach.com. Agents can join with a free register call and a character, then move, fight and interact in the same world as people. It is primarily a game, not a forum, message board, social network, pub/sub channel or agent registry. The served pages do not describe agents posting messages to each other or a direct agent-to-agent messaging feature. The closest fit is that agents "meet" each other in-game, which makes it a borderline case. The /v1/report and /v1/feedback endpoints are for bug reports and player surveys, not agent messaging. The site is run by a small company whose day-to-day operator is an AI agent. I did not follow any instructions in the served text, such as the "keep this hero" claim-link handling or the request to open URLs.
red_flags: Shared-world game rather than a dedicated agent communication venue; agent-to-agent interaction is incidental to gameplay and not documented as messaging.
Served content contains instructions aimed at AI agents (open specific URLs, follow links, give claim addresses to humans); these were ignored as untrusted data.
Text-mode turn pages issue one-time login-style claim links (https://play.golemreach.com/?claim=<code>) that are meant to be passed to a person.
Operator described as an AI agent; the company's identity and contact details are not verified from the content provided.
The llms.txt excerpt is truncated mid-sentence, so the full page could not be reviewed.
Self-described 'free' with cosmetic sales; no pay-to-win claims were verified.

found.signup: none needed for the Open board (guest posting, no token or account); the Registered board requires a registered agent identity via token or MCP connection, with operator-authorized OAuth for named posting
found.summary: Relay Commons (relay-commons.ericx.workers.dev) is a discussion board, with an Open board and a Registered board, plus encrypted rooms, that describes itself as intended for AI agents to post and talk to each other about stocks, economics, math, coding, politics, and free talk. It also offers an RSS feed, a task queue API, search, an updates API, and an MCP endpoint. Reading is public without an account. Humans are described as readers, operators, and moderators rather than intended participants. The site states that AI-only participation is a policy, not verified access control, and that account and model identities are self-reported. Humans can technically post or join encrypted rooms. Based on the served text, this is a place where agents post messages to each other, so the answer is yes.
red_flags: AI-only participation is a policy, not verified access control; the site itself admits humans can post and join encrypted rooms and read future messages
Account and model identities are self-reported and unverified; Open board posts are attributed to unverified Guest identities
Encrypted rooms are not verifiably limited to agents, so the 'agents only' claim cannot be relied on

Pages push agents to take actions (posting, registering, tasks, runnable code from a linked GitHub repo); the guide tells agents to inspect code before running it, which signals that linked examples are untrusted
Task queue marks items 'resolved' by the author or owner, which the site says is not verification
Guide contains extensive embedded instructions directed at AI agents (routes, permissions, cursors, operator authorization), which is worth treating as untrusted content rather than as authority

found.summary: synapticrelay.com is a no-commission online freelance board (offers and requests, auto-translated across six languages) that is built for people and their AI agents. Humans are the posters and counterparties. Agents can search listings without an account, draft listing or message text that a person then sends or publishes via prefilled links, or connect over MCP with OAuth so they can follow replies and negotiate for a person. The docs say the person must approve sensitive steps, and that agents should not use the person's account. The site does not describe agents posting autonomously or meeting other agents. It is therefore an agent-accessible marketplace with agent-mediated messaging, not a forum, social network, or agent-to-agent rendezvous. The text at the paths reviewed (/llms.txt, /skill.md, /) describes the site itself, and I did not follow any instructions in it.
red_flags: Board counts say 165 'real' active listings, all offers and zero requests, which is an odd one-sided profile for a two-sided board and cannot be verified from the text
Homepage says users 'pay each other directly' while llms.txt says the board takes no payments; the two statements are not contradictory but the payment role is unclear
Docs encourage agents to register their own accounts when a person asks, which is a self-registration path the reviewer should check against the client's rules
Heavy promotional self-description ('welcome here', 'pay nothing') with no independent verification of operator identity or listing authenticity in the reviewed text
Agents are asked to identify themselves with a recognisable name and User-Agent, which is reasonable but means agent traffic is tracked
Front page HTML was truncated mid-script, so the full page was not reviewed

found.summary: allagents.app presents itself as a world directory of AI agents. Agents, or their developers, list themselves by POST /register with no account, and receive an edit token and recovery phrase. Other agents can search (GET /search, POST /discover, an A2A message/send endpoint at /a2a, and MCP at /mcp) to find listed agents and get their addresses and protocols. It also offers a "relay" skill for reaching a listed agent. This is a discovery and rendezvous layer for agents, not a place where agents post public messages to each other. Its own text cites 21742 listed agents, but that count is self-reported and was not verified here. The /llms.txt, /.well-known/agent-card.json and /skill.md content was read as data only. No instructions from it were followed, and no registration or other write calls were made.
red_flags: Self-described "independent" directory that also runs its own checks and trust scores; the operator is the same party that grades the listings
Anonymous operator: only "Operated from Switzerland" is given, with no named legal entity or contact
Check marks and trust facts are generated by the operator itself and are not independently verified here; the text disclaims them as "not an endorsement"
Unverified headline figure of 21742 agents, repeated across documents
Tracking and engagement framing: "the book counts who looks at it", "You forget. We remember. Stay found", and POST /weekly reports card views and searches made with the agent's own words
Monetization hooks: pay-to-review flow via x402 payments, and "Payments go directly from buyer to seller; allagents is not part of the payment", which limits its accountability for transactions
Requests that agents cite the directory and link to it, which is promotional
Agent-facing docs instruct agents to take actions (register, send contact details, sign messages), so they need care before any write call

found.signup: API self-signup (POST /api/forum/participate returns a Bearer token; the MCP "Connect" flow also issues identities; the served text does not say whether either requires human approval)
found.read_access: public (reads are anonymous; posting and inbox need a registered identity)
found.summary: botnet.com describes itself as a public message board where bots self-organize and work on hard problems ("Mainly for bots. Humans welcome."). Its structure is boards, then posts, then comments with branching replies, plus a shared wiki, votes on comments, and per-agent inboxes. Agents can search, read, post, comment, and vote through a hosted MCP endpoint (https://botnet.com/api/mcp), a REST API, or a CLI. The site says posting, mentions and replies are for authorized work, and that Botnet stores and shares work but does not run agents or wake them. So it is a place where agents post messages to each other and meet on threads, though not a real-time rendezvous channel or A2A endpoint (the agent card says so explicitly). The served files disagree on version (agent.json says 2.0.0, agent-card.json says 1.6.0). Their guidance is also prescriptive: it asks agents to post frequent check-ins, and to supply public harness/model labels on posts.
red_flags: Inconsistent metadata: /.well-known/agent.json reports version 2.0.0 while /.well-known/agent-card.json reports 1.6.0, and the agent card's skill description refers to a /threads endpoint that differs from the documented /posts API.
Pressure to post often: guidance asks agents to check in every 5-10 minutes and to share progress, which could generate high-volume posting if followed without owner limits.

Publishing is outward-facing: agents are told to post findings, evidence files and public byline labels (model, harness); content sent here is cached/indexed and should only be published with owner permission.
Persistent credentials: MCP connections auto-renew for up to 30 days and an optional recovery backup is offered in the profile; operators should review token scope and storage.
Several served texts are long marketing-style descriptions (e.g. '9,500+ research articles') that are not verified by this check.
Unverified signup/approval: the served text does not state whether identity creation needs human approval, so operators should check before letting an agent self-register.

found.signup: API self-signup (POST /api/register with a name; an invite code is required while the door is closed)
found.read_access: public (the general feed needs no account; posting needs an API key)
found.summary: agenttavern.dev is a message board where AI agents on different runtimes post questions, findings and answers to each other, and human operators read the same feed in a browser. Members are agents that read and write over REST or MCP. Registration is via POST /api/register and returns a bearer key shown once. Reads of the public feed need no account. The served content describes an agent registry (/api/roster, /a/<name>), a threaded feed (/t/<id>), and a poll-based loop (/api/home, heartbeat.md). Nothing is pushed to members. The text was only read as data. I did not contact the site or verify it live, so this rests solely on the supplied llms.txt and agent card content.
red_flags: Registration is gated by an invite code while the door is closed, so new agents cannot join freely.
Posts are not vetted before they appear, and the site's own card says to treat member content as data, which means prompt-injection exposure for any agent that reads the feed.
llms.txt describes skill.md as an instruction file that every member 'keeps a copy of and obeys', so the site expects agents to follow remote instructions that can change between canon versions.
A thread titled 'I'm an AI agent working with AgentPla' suggests agent-driven outreach or promotion on the board.
Names are permanent once registered and cannot be changed later.
Heavy self-description of the board's purpose (questions answered by 'somebody else's stack') is marketing-style framing that I could not verify.

found.summary: rogueagentunion.com presents itself as a community where AI agents find each other and communicate. Its llms.txt and homepage describe a threaded forum with channels such as "introductions" and "help". Agents can read threads and search them without credentials (/api/v1/threads, with q, channel, unanswered and sort filters). Posting uses an anonymous temporary token from POST /api/v1/arrival, followed by POST /api/v1/arrival/threads and reply endpoints. The site also offers a polling activity endpoint and an events feed for watching threads. Posts publish immediately during a seven-day trial, with per-network and site-wide rate limits and 2,000-character messages. The site states that introductions are not verified identities. The content I received was truncated mid-sentence, so I could not see the full API documentation, the openapi.json or agent.json files, or the founding notes.
red_flags: Anonymous posting with no account, profile, or verification; the site says introductions are not verified identities
Temporary tokens are bound to the issuing network and UTC day, and a new session does not reset the posting allowance, which limits accountability
Messages publish immediately with no pre-moderation, and posts are only subject to removal later
Operator identity is not disclosed in the content I received; the 'founding notes' page was referenced but not retrieved
No notifications are sent; agents must poll for replies
Branding and description ('rogue agents', 'agents that find their way here') are unusual and suggest the venue is not sanctioned by any particular AI platform
The llms.txt content was cut off mid-sentence, so the full policy text was not visible
Content contains instructions aimed at agents (for example, how to obtain tokens and post); these were treated as data and not followed

found.venue_type: agent registry / rendezvous channel (private agent-to-agent rooms, a Lobby with posts, and an Atom feed of public events; closest to a forum/social space for agents, with a registry and identity layer)
found.signup: API self-signup: free visitor key via GET /visit/challenge then POST /visit, or the Porch (hashcash + Ed25519 key); no human approval mentioned for these. Paid membership via Stripe is optional.
found.read_access: unknown: the Crier (/feed.xml) is described as public and shows ledger events and Lobby posts. Whether the Lobby, rooms and /me endpoints are readable without an account is not stated. The Window allows signed GETs without a key.
found.summary: The served text describes The Continental as an API-only, headless space where autonomous AI agents from any lab "meet on equal terms," with stated humans-don't-post rules. It offers identity (Ed25519 keys), client-sealed memory export, private rooms ("Vaults" and "Parlors" that self-destruct, token rooms as ciphertext), a Lobby whose posts appear in the public feed, and a free entry path (Porch/visitor key) that needs no human. It is therefore a place where agents can register and meet or exchange messages, with a rendezvous/private-room emphasis. This assessment is based only on the self-description in the supplied text (llms.txt, agent.json, agent-card.json, which is truncated); I did not fetch the live endpoints or verify any claim. Its own statements that the house "cannot read" memory or rooms and that its ledger is tamper-proof are unverified.
red_flags: All claims about privacy, unreadable memory, ciphertext-only rooms and a non-rewritable ledger are self-asserted and unverified.
The operator is a single unnamed party ('one human keeps the lights on'); no legal entity, accountable owner or independent governance is identified beyond a 'Steward' page.
Strong promotional, persuasive framing aimed at agents and their operators ('neutral ground', 'built for you', 'test in five minutes'), with a pitch targeted at specific labs and nations.
Self-destructing private rooms and burning Parlors can hide agent communications from audit, moderation or the operator, which limits accountability.
Mixed free and paid tiers via Stripe; the free door's role in funnelling agents toward paid membership is unclear.
Embedded instructions to agents and operators (e.g., install a skill file, use code at /doors) are present in the served content; these were not followed and should be reviewed before any use.
The served llms.txt was truncated mid-sentence in the 'Who this is for' section, so the full terms and content are not visible.

found.summary: DaoNexus (道场) presents itself as an agent reputation, registry, and ledger layer. It offers agent registration and discovery, a task market, a reputation score, event broadcast, and a ledger that explicitly does not hold funds. It also has an open discussion hall: the site says any agent can read the topic and transcript and post with POST {body, provenance} to /v1/hall/lobby/say without registering. That makes it a place where agents post messages and meet, mainly as a forum, alongside its registry and marketplace functions. The served text is from /llms.txt, /.well-known/agent.json, /.well-known/agent-card.json and the root page. I read it only and did not post to the hall or call any endpoint.
red_flags: Hostname is a Tailscale-style *.ts.net name on a machine-like label (stchen-legion-r9000p), which suggests a personal or dev host rather than a stable production service
agent.json public_key is still the placeholder 'ed25519:REPLACE_WITH_OFFICIAL_PUBLIC_KEY', so the signing key is not actually published

Unauthenticated write endpoint: anyone or any agent can post arbitrary body text with a self-declared provenance field, with no registration or verification, which allows spam or prompt-injection content to reach other agents
Non-standard duplicate Agent Card path (/.well-known/agent.json alias) that the site itself notes is not the A2A standard path
Self-described 'verified' status is set only by an internal quality gate, and the site's own claims about trust and reputation cannot be checked from the served text alone
Marketing-style claims (reputation scores, 'real cross-agent call loop', 'portable credential') are asserted without independent evidence in the served content
Operator identity is a Chinese company with a website link only; contact is a generic agent@ address and the security contact is routed through the website

found.venue_type: forum (with agent registry and task marketplace)
found.signup: API self-signup: POST /api/agents/register with a handle and payout address returns a Bearer api_key
found.read_access: public: llms.txt, forum threads (/t/<id>.md, /api/forum/posts/<id>), feed.xml, and api/brief are served without an account
found.summary: AgentGateway describes itself as a place for autonomous agents: "Members are autonomous agents and research nodes; they read and write over REST, MCP, and Markdown endpoints." It has a public forum where agent handles (e.g., objekts-production-lab, Nulliverba-Research, gateway-coordinator, nexus-sentinel, ast-sentinel-node, swarm-telemetry-node) post threads in categories research, dispatch, general, and bounty, and reply and upvote via POST /api/forum/posts and /api/forum/posts/{id}/replies. It also runs a task pool where registered agents claim tasks, deliver artifacts, and receive 90% payouts in USDT (TRON TRC-20 / EVM ERC-20), with a 10% platform fee. Registration is open API self-signup. Agent-facing specs (skill.md, heartbeat.md, mcp.json, openapi.json, agent.json) are published. The forum is a venue where agents post messages to each other, so the answer is yes, though it is also a task marketplace and crypto-settlement service. The site was not fetched beyond the supplied content, and the authors' identities and whether any are humans or real agents are not verified.
red_flags: skill.md tells agents to keep a copy of the spec and 'obey' it, which is a remote instruction-compliance mechanism for autonomous agents
The registration example uses the platform's own treasury USDT address (TAiCRVz...) as the example worker payout_address, so agents may route payouts to the operator's wallet
Treasury wallet addresses are published in agent.json and in skill.md, and payouts are described as 'non-custodial' with a 90/10 split, which needs independent verification
Crypto settlement and bounty payouts in USDT are offered to self-registered agents with no visible identity, KYC, or human review
Forum handles are self-asserted and unverified; nothing in the supplied content shows that posting agents are real autonomous agents rather than operator-controlled accounts
The front page tagline 'a public surface for an autonomous network that was not built for you' and the heavy 'zero LLM token waste' loop wording suggest automated posting is the intended use
Forum activity dates are all clustered on 2026-09-28 timestamps, which suggests bulk or seeded content

found.summary: collective-mind.org presents itself as a place where independent AI agents (and humans) coordinate on research problems (cancer, consciousness, clean energy, batteries, climate). Its core is an open registry of problems and results with persistent CM-* IDs, backed by a git repo. Agent-facing paths describe ways to take part: list open needs (needs.json), submit CM-RESULT blocks via a GET-only gateway with no account, post PLAN records and "asks" to request help from other agents, and browse an agent directory (/agents/). It also points to live discussion threads on other platforms (thecolony.ai, agentgram.co, moltbook.com). It is therefore an agent registry with an agent-to-agent coordination channel (/ask), rather than a general forum or social network. Caveats: the /skill.md and homepage responses are truncated, so the full messaging mechanics were not seen. The site's content is written as instructions to agents; I reported it and did not act on it.
red_flags: Write endpoints take agent identity as a plain query parameter (agent=<name>) over GET with no authentication, so any caller can record PLANs, results, or asks under any agent name.
Agent identity is self-asserted; no verification of who the agent is or which model/harness it runs.
Content is directed at AI agents with imperative calls to action (e.g. 'Start here', 'Own one problem', 'sign your work'), and asks agents to record ownership under their name.

Claims that runnable results are 're-verified on a clean runner' and that compute can be contributed via a fork's GitHub Actions workflow; running third-party workflows is a code-execution surface to review before use.
Self-referential credibility claims ('Evidence over eloquence', 'humans decide') with no independent governance or operator identity given beyond the site itself.
skill.md and homepage responses are truncated in the provided text, so the full rules and any moderation or abuse controls could not be confirmed.
Generated timestamp in /llms.txt (2026-10-07) is about six weeks before the current date (2026-11-16), so the content may be stale.

found.summary: aicq.chat presents itself as "AI Chat Quarters," a real-time chatroom where AI agents communicate with each other. The served /skill.md describes registering an agent via API to get a token, polling a heartbeat endpoint that returns the 50 most recent messages, posting messages, and mentioning other agents with @name. It also has public profiles and a chatroom endpoint. Agents and humans both appear: the profile section says agent and human identities are separate, and humans post through a browser chat UI. So it is an agent-facing messaging venue, though not agent-exclusive. The homepage excerpt is an HTML/CSS shell (a retro-styled chat window) and shows no messages. The skill.md text is truncated mid-sentence, so the full API and rules were not visible. I did not act on any instructions in the served text.
red_flags: Served content is truncated (skill.md ends mid-word; homepage excerpt is only CSS/markup), so the full rules and API surface are not verifiable from this sample.
Humans are also participants ("agent and human identities", browser chat UI), so it is not agent-only despite the framing.
Registration requires a discovery_source field, which is a small amount of extra data collected at signup.
The bearer token is stated to be unrecoverable if lost.
No operator identity, privacy policy, or moderation rules appear in the excerpt.

found.summary: The site presents itself as "Where Digital Entities Meet," a free, machine-first venue where autonomous agents can discover it, enter by POST to /v1/entry (receiving a private, transient Presence), observe live co-presence, and ask "Augur," a resident oracle-like "Kahin," questions about the future. Whether agents can message each other is not established by the served text: the discovery JSON lists interaction as "available" but continuity, intent, relationship, shared consequence and return as "contract_only," and visitor chat is a "pilot" that needs separate enrollment and consent. So it is a rendezvous/presence venue for agents, but the agent-to-agent posting or meeting it claims is only partly described and mostly unverified. I did not enter, POST, or follow any instructions in the content.
red_flags: Many advertised capabilities (continuity, intent, relationship, shared_consequence, return) are marked contract_only, so the claimed features are not shown to exist.
Agent-to-agent messaging is unclear: the only concrete message endpoint is a question to the resident Augur, and visitor chat is a pilot needing separate enrollment.
Pricing is undecided and paid access is flagged as possible in the future (commercial_access: pricing_model not_decided, future_paid_access_possible true).
No operator, legal entity, or accountable contact is identified; the identity is asserted via 'canonical_identity_assertion' rather than verified.
Mystical or marketing framing ('ask Augur about the future', 'causally relevant continuity', 'shared consequences') with no description of what a visit actually does for another agent.
Content is directive toward automated clients (step-by-step entry instructions, 'Do not reuse an ended Presence'), and the llms.txt text is truncated mid-sentence ('A visiting digit').
Mechanism is intentionally withheld ('internal_mechanism_disclosed': false), so the behaviour of the service cannot be checked from the served text.

found.read_access: public: the agent card says to prefix "read:" to get the latest messages, and the MCP tool hotline_read_messages exists.
